title: The slow plans: c3, d3 and the Giuoco Pianissimo
outcomes: Says what the pawn move c3 prepares (d4 with a pawn recapture, control of b4) and what d3 prepares (a safe e4, the bishop on c1), and what each costs
Names the retreat squares of the bishop on c4 before and after d3, and picks the retreat that keeps the diagonal, the rook and the pawns working
Describes White's quiet set-up (knight d2, a4, h3, rook e1, bishop b3) and Black's replies, with what each move makes possible later
Counts the attackers and defenders of d4 before a break, and tells a ready break from a premature one
Spots the typical mistakes (d4 too early, a second bishop move into an exchange, ...Ng4 against h3) and Black's ...d5 at the right moment
Quotes our own counts for the quiet moves, with their sample sizes, and says what the counts do and do not show

steps.caption: Move 4, White to move. Each side has a knight and a bishop out, and the pawns on e4 and e5 face each other. White has three quiet ideas: a pawn to c3, a pawn to d3, or castling. Do not look for a tactic. Which pawn move would you play first, and would you play the other one too?

steps.prompt: Before any explanation, even if you are unsure: which pawn move would you play first, c3 or d3, and would you play the other one too? You will come back to this at the end.

fields.label: The other move, yes or no, and why:

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** The pawn moves c3 and d3 are both quiet, and the engine rates them about equally. Yet they prepare different things. By the end you can say what each prepares, how the pieces stand in the quiet structure that follows, how Black answers, and which mistakes cost something. The method is always the same: ask what a move makes possible later, then check it on a board.

steps.text: **Two jobs for the pawn on c3.** It controls d4, so a later d4 can be met by a recapture with a pawn, and White keeps two pawns in the middle. It also controls b4. The price: c3 does nothing for e4, so after the knight attack White must choose between guarding it and striking at once. [I] That choice decides which plan White is playing.

steps.text: **Three jobs for the pawn on d3.** It guards e4 for good, so the knight's attack on it costs nothing. It frees the bishop on c1 for g5 or e3. And it keeps the centre closed, so d4 can wait until the pieces are ready. [H] The quiet move buys time to choose a set-up; I do not know why masters play it, and our counts later show only that c3 and d3 are both common.

steps.caption: The two moves do different jobs, so most players play both: c3 prepares d4 and the push b4; d3 guards e4 and frees the bishop on c1. [I] Playing c3 first keeps the option of d4 for one more move. Step through the usual order.

steps.text: **What d3 costs, honestly.** Before d3 the bishop could retreat to b3, d3, e2 or f1. After d3 only b3 remains, so ...b5 or ...Na5 gains Black a move. [I] The next board shows the engine is happy with that retreat, so this price is small. [H] The bigger prices are slower play, less space, and an easier ...d5 for Black. Capablanca judged a set-up by its concessions; engines sometimes overturn that rule of thumb. [S]

steps.prompt: Three retreats, four results. In one sentence: what did the best retreats keep that the weaker ones lost?

steps.text: **What a retreat has to keep: a checklist.** Does the bishop keep a useful diagonal? Does the rook keep its guard of e4? Is the d-pawn free to move? Bb3 passed all three. Bf1 gave up the diagonal but passed the other two. Each of the other retreats failed one. [I] This is my reading of a few positions, a checklist of trade-offs, not a law. Once d3 is played the structure itself picks the retreat.

steps.caption: The quiet structure on one board (the Giuoco Pianissimo, after six moves each). Switch on the control map and look at b4, d4, d5 and f5. White's pawns form two short chains, from b2 to c3 and from d3 to e4. Black has one chain, from c7 to d6 to e5.

steps.text: **Reading the skeleton.** Edward Lasker argued that pieces can retreat but pawns cannot, so the pawn skeleton is what lasts and the pieces should be placed around it. [S] Nimzowitsch advised removing a strong enemy centre pawn by a *prepared* pawn break. [S] Here White's break is d4, which needs support. Black's break is ...d5, which needs e4 overloaded. Both breaks stay in reserve while pieces are placed.

steps.text: **What these moves promise.** The knight on d2 and the rook on e1 give e4 three guards, so the knight can later leave d2 and the centre stays safe. The pawn on h3 answers the pin, and the pawn on a4 stops ...b5. Together they free White to choose a plan. Nimzowitsch defended quiet moves that put pieces on key points. [S] [I] The cost of quiet insurance is time.

steps.text: **White's plans in the quiet structure.** Make e4 safe first: a knight, a rook and the pawn on h3. Then choose a route for the knight: the square c4 once the bishop has left it, or the kingside through f1. [H] Gain space on the queenside when Black's bishop can be kicked. Break in the centre only when Black's pieces cannot punish it. [I] The order matters more than the list.

**Black's plans.** Keep e5 solid with a pawn on d6 and a rook behind it. Keep the bishop alive: give it a retreat square and stop the pin. Challenge White's bishop with a bishop trade or a knight to a5. Break with the pawn push to d5 only when two pieces stand behind it and e5 will not fall. [I] Neither side needs a forcing plan, only a safe one.

steps.text: **What strong players chose** (our data; counts of choices, not verdicts). [V] After the bishop reaches c5, in the 7,112 master games listed: c3 in 3,134 games (White scored 55.7%), d3 in 1,964 (53.8%), castling in 1,580 (54.1%). After c3 and the knight move: d3 in 2,264, d4 in 777. A win counts one, a draw half. [H] Scores this close suggest the choices are close in quality.

**Club games look different.** Online, rating band 1500 to 1700 (15,626 games reach this position): c3 in 4,485 games (White scored 53.7%), d3 in 3,324 (49.9%), castling in 3,258 (51.0%). After c3 and the knight move: d4 in 1,453 of 2,660 games, d3 in 768. [V] After c3 and the knight move, masters choose d3 about three times as often as d4; club players choose d4 about twice as often as d3. Online data is not master theory.

Teach it back. Imagine you teach a friend who knows how the pieces move. Write five sentences: (1) what the pawn move c3 prepares, (2) what d3 prepares and what it costs, (3) one position they could set up on a board, (4) one warning (a mistake from this lesson), (5) what Black does in reply.

steps.text: **Self-check.** Did you say when the break d4 works (a pawn can recapture, few attackers) and when it fails (two attackers, a blocked queen)? Did you give an example a friend could set up on a board? Did you name one mistake from this lesson? Then go back to your first guess at the start of the lesson and change one word.

**One model teach-back** (my wording; yours can differ). (1) c3 prepares d4, because a pawn can recapture there. (2) d3 guards e4 and frees the bishop, but leaves the bishop on c4 one retreat. (3) Set up White's pawns on c3, d3 and e4, a knight on d2 and a rook on e1. (4) Warning: d4 too early loses a pawn when two pieces attack it. (5) Black guards e5, stops the pin, and plays ...d5 only with support.

steps.prompt: Did your teach-back pass the self-check? Which of the five sentences was the weakest?

steps.text:
**What to remember: ideas.**
- c3 prepares d4 with a pawn recapture; it does nothing for e4. The two moves do different jobs, so most players play both.
- d3 guards e4 and frees the bishop on c1, but leaves the bishop on c4 one retreat.
- Check what a retreat keeps: the diagonal, the rook's guard of e4, the free d-pawn. [I]
- Quiet insurance first, then a plan.

**What to remember: breaks and numbers.**
- Break with d4 only when few pieces attack it; break with ...d5 when two pieces stand behind it. [I] (in the positions checked here)
- At move 4 masters choose c3 most (3,134 of 7,112 games). After 4.c3 Nf6 they choose d3 about three times as often as d4 (2,264 vs 777); club players choose d4 about twice as often as d3. [V]
